img-0.jpeg.description:
This is an architectural diagram of a Transformer model, showing both the encoder (left) and decoder (right) components. 

The encoder (left side) processes inputs through:
- Input Embedding layer at the bottom
- Positional Encoding (added via ⊕ symbol)
- N× stacked blocks, each containing:
  - Masked Multi-Head Attention (orange)
  - Add & Norm layer (yellow)
  - Feed Forward layer (blue)
  - Another Add & Norm layer (yellow)
- Residual connections shown as curved arrows around each sub-layer

The decoder (right side) processes outputs (shifted right) through:
- Output Embedding layer
- Positional Encoding (added via ⊕ symbol)
- N× stacked blocks, each containing:
  - Masked Multi-Head Attention (orange)
  - Add & Norm layer (yellow)
  - Multi-Head Attention that receives input from encoder (orange)
  - Add & Norm layer (yellow)
  - Feed Forward layer (blue)
  - Add & Norm layer (yellow)
- Residual connections around each sub-layer

The decoder output flows through:
- Linear layer (gray)
- Softmax layer (green)
- Final Output Probabilities

This diagram illustrates the classic "Attention is All You Need" Transformer architecture, showing the parallel processing structure, residual connections, and the flow of information from inputs to output probabilities.

img-1.jpeg.description:
This image shows a technical comparison diagram of two attention mechanisms used in neural networks: Scaled Dot-Product Attention (left) and Multi-Head Attention (right).

Left side - Scaled Dot-Product Attention:
The diagram shows a vertical flow chart with the following sequential operations:
1. Three inputs at the bottom: Q (Query), K (Key), and V (Value)
2. MatMul operation combining Q and K
3. Scale operation
4. Mask (opt.) - optional masking step shown in pink
5. SoftMax operation shown in green
6. MatMul operation combining with V (shown in purple)
7. Output arrow at the top

Right side - Multi-Head Attention:
The diagram illustrates a parallel architecture with:
1. Three inputs at the bottom: V, K, and Q
2. Three parallel Linear transformation layers for each input
3. Multiple parallel Scaled Dot-Product Attention blocks (shown as stacked layers with 'h' indicating the number of heads)
4. Concat operation (shown in yellow) that combines outputs from all attention heads
5. Final Linear transformation layer
6. Output arrow at the top

The visualization effectively demonstrates how Multi-Head Attention uses multiple parallel attention mechanisms (indicated by the stacked/layered appearance) compared to the single-path Scaled Dot-Product Attention, which is a fundamental architectural difference in transformer models.

img-2.jpeg.description:
This image shows a comparative diagram illustrating the difficulty in voter registration or voting processes across two time periods. The diagram consists of two parallel triangular/funnel-shaped visualizations stacked vertically.

Both sections contain identical text that reads: "It is in this spirit that a majority of American governments have passed new laws since 2009 making the registration or voting process more difficult."

Key visual elements:
- The text is arranged in a curved, flowing pattern following the shape of triangular forms
- Color coding is used to highlight specific words: "more" appears in blue/cyan, and "difficult" appears in red/orange in the lower diagram
- Multiple arrow symbols (‹EOS›, ‹pad›) appear on the right side of both diagrams, suggesting this may be related to natural language processing or text generation analysis
- The triangular shapes create a visual funnel effect, possibly representing the narrowing or restriction of voting access

The dual presentation suggests a before/after comparison or demonstrates how the same text is processed or analyzed in different ways. The color highlighting of "more difficult" emphasizes the key concern about increased barriers to voting. This appears to be from a technical or academic analysis of voting rights legislation or text processing of political discourse.

img-3.jpeg.description:
This is a word alignment visualization diagram showing three different representations of the same sentence alignment. The diagram displays how words in one sentence (top row) map to words in another sentence (bottom row) through connecting lines. The sentence reads "The Law will never be perfect , but its application should be just - this is what we are missing , in my opinion . <EOS> <pad>".

The visualization shows three versions:
1. Top panel: A complex alignment pattern with multiple purple lines of varying opacity connecting words between the top and bottom sequences, showing many-to-many word correspondences
2. Middle panel: A simplified version highlighting specific alignment connections, with a gray box emphasizing the "application" region
3. Bottom panel: Shows the base sequences with colored boxes (purple for "Law" and beige for "application") at the bottom, with minimal connecting lines

This type of diagram is commonly used in natural language processing and machine translation research to visualize attention mechanisms or word alignment patterns between parallel texts. The <EOS> (end of sequence) and <pad> (padding) tokens indicate this is from a neural network model output.

img-4.jpeg.description:
This image shows two parallel coordinate plots or alignment diagrams comparing text sequences, displayed in green (top) and red (bottom). Each plot connects words or tokens between two horizontal lines, showing relationships or alignments between corresponding elements in what appears to be a sentence or phrase.

The text sequence reads: "The Law will never be perfect , but its application should be just - this is what we are missing , in my opinion . <EOS> <pad>"

Key features:
- Green lines (top diagram): Show connections between words in the upper and lower sequences, with varying line intensities (darker lines indicate stronger connections)
- Red lines (bottom diagram): Display a different set of alignments for the same text, also with varying intensities
- The diagrams appear to be comparing different alignment or attention patterns, possibly from a neural network model or machine translation system
- Special tokens like <EOS> (end of sentence) and <pad> (padding) are included at the end
- Line opacity/intensity variations suggest weighted connections or attention scores between word pairs
- This type of visualization is commonly used in natural language processing to show word alignments, attention mechanisms, or translation correspondences
